searchText: i'm not sure if this is appropriate for this channel, but i've just run into a situation which i think warrents some thought. I deposited to Spadina and thought all is well cause I saw the 'Deposit' event log. Little did I realize that my deposits were in fact invalid. How do we prevent this loss of funds and even more so, the inability to validate after such a mistake ? in my case I believe after using a client's auto deposit function thru geth, I simply forgot to add the testnet flag. Which I realize isn't a real world scenario, but still it's concering you'd get a 'normal' deposit log statement on Eth1, yet be completely invalid on Eth2 Best approach would be to prepare your deposit with an audited tool like the deposit-cli, and verifying the deposit before submitting it to deposit contract on eth1 with actual value. <@!203220829473996800> how does one even do that? and where do we tell people they need to when clients implement an auto wallet creation->to deposit user experience not realizing such a mess can occur Clients should definitely improve the deposit flow, to avoid confusing testnets, or having bad defaults looking at etherscan.io everything looks green, contract result seems good, it's all so misleading and it would be one thing if one just didn't get to validate, but the loss of funds, makes for a very tricky situation (if this were to happen to people in real life) fully agree there, but need clients to improve here, to protect better from user errors I agree with that statement, but it feels like the deposit contract should be a bit beefier, and send back funds that are attached to deposits that are invalid giving back a good result, while in fact it's invalid, and one that forfeits the funds, is not an acceptable flow in any way unfortunately the deposit contract cannot do signature verification at the moment <@!489217181104734219> Yea, that's been discussed, no BLS on eth1 is a problem holding that back can there be a function in the contract that is only allowed to be accessible by the beacon chain, causing a kick back of funds to invalid deposits ? Aside from improving the situation on the Eth1 chain, the best approach would be to prepare your deposits as json, and double-check them with other tools, before actually submitting them. And preferably use audited tools meaing beacon chain does signature verification, and causes an event on ETH1 chain ? how would you allow a function to be accessible only by the beacon nodes? eth1 doesnt know anything about eth2, no way to differentiate any external actors from others unless they have a verifiable eth1 address such as contract owner or admin <@!203220829473996800> that's all logical, and def something I'll do better next time. But I am here every day and managed to get it wrong... do you think people who will be jumping on the hype will know where to find which tools are audited and which aren't? hell I don't even know which tools are audited and which aren't... and one would think that the "clients" are all audited by the mere virtue of them being the sanctioned clients a potential solution is to discourage any deposit tools that are not the eth2.0-deposit-cli <@!311971895828283393> good point we are going to remove all deposit tools from Prysm soon, for example and _only_ allow for launchpad or eth2 deposit cli <@!311971895828283393> this happened with lighthouse, so no worries about prysm 😉 we should be narrowing down the process but it couldve easily happened with Prysm as well <@!311971895828283393> the bug i opened before on prysm about this is what prevented me from using prysm for it 😉 by encouraging users to use the eth2 deposit cli as the canonical method, it will solve this problem <@!311971895828283393> agreed, the process should def be narrowed down > by encouraging users to use the eth2 deposit cli as the canonical method, it will solve this problem <@!311971895828283393> +1, this sounds very logical what we can't trust or leave to chance is for people to find out on their own what is and isn't audited, that's no way to go hell to this day it's not even clear what some mechanism were finally used and weren't used in ETH2 given the amount of talk over the years e.g: CBC What I'm still missing is an official, tested and audited tool for depositing larger numbers of validators. I funded 1100 validators via the launch pad which took me 2 hours of clicking in the launch pad and confirming things in metamask. Ended up with 3 double deposits.

excerpts.author: schone_wizard
excerpts.content: i'm not sure if this is appropriate for this channel, but i've just run into a situation which i think warrents some thought.  I deposited to Spadina and thought all is well cause I saw the 'Deposit' event log.  Little did I realize that my deposits were in fact invalid.  How do we prevent this loss of funds and even more so, the inability to validate after such a mistake ?

excerpts.author: schone_wizard
excerpts.content: in my case I believe after using a client's auto deposit function thru geth, I simply forgot to add the testnet flag.  Which I realize isn't a real world scenario, but still it's concering you'd get a 'normal' deposit log statement on Eth1, yet be completely invalid on Eth2

excerpts.author: protolambda
excerpts.content: Best approach would be to prepare your deposit with an audited tool like the deposit-cli, and verifying the deposit before submitting it to deposit contract on eth1 with actual value.

excerpts.author: schone_wizard
excerpts.content: <@!203220829473996800> how does one even do that? and where do we tell people they need to when clients implement an auto wallet creation->to deposit user experience not realizing such a mess can occur

excerpts.content: Clients should definitely improve the deposit flow, to avoid confusing testnets, or having bad defaults
